title: 道德經 第六十章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 60, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 82. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 60 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 居位 (Occupying the Throne). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: to govern, to put in order
to boil, to cook in a pot
fresh — and here the adjective stands in for the thing: the fresh-caught, a small fish

sentences.l:
Governing a great state —
like cooking a small fish.
sentences.n:
The whole chapter hangs on this image, and Wang Bi puts the point in two characters: 不擾也 — 'do not stir it'. A small fish turned about in the pan comes apart; a great state handled the same way comes apart the same way. He adds: the larger the state, the stiller its ruler.

大國 and 小鮮 stay two words each. They mean exactly what their parts mean — great + state, small + fresh-thing — and nothing in the text christens them, so the reader taps each character on its own. Compare 天下 in the next line, which really is one word.

sentences.t:
以道莅天下，
其鬼不神；

morph.gloss: to come and take one's place above, to preside over — a ruler's word
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world, and everyone in it
a ghost — the dead who linger, and the malignant powers of a place
to work spirit-power, to be numinous — the NOUN 'spirit' doing a verb's work here

sentences.l:
By the Way to preside over all-under-heaven —
its ghosts do not work as spirits.
sentences.i: Preside over all under heaven by the Way, and its ghosts do not act as spirits.
sentences.n:
莅 is a ruler's word: to come and stand above a people, to preside. Some witnesses write the plainer 立 'to stand' in its place — the same word with a simpler graph, which is how a great many of the book's variants arise.

鬼 and 神 are the two halves of the unseen world: 鬼 the dead who have not gone quietly and the powers that haunt a place, 神 the gods and the numinous force working in things. Here 神 is a noun doing a verb's work — 'to be numinous, to work as a spirit'. Two lines on it will be a plain noun again, in the same chapter, with nothing but its position to tell you which.

sentences.t:
非其鬼不神，
其神不傷人；

morph.gloss: it is not the case that — 非 denies a whole statement or a noun, where 不 negates a verb
spirit-power, the numinous in them — now a plain NOUN
to wound, to do harm to

sentences.l:
Not that its ghosts do not work as spirits —
their spirit-power does not harm men.
sentences.i: It is not that the ghosts do not act as spirits; it is that their spirit-power does men no harm.
sentences.n:
非 and 不 are not interchangeable, and the difference carries this whole chapter. 不 negates a verb — 'does not harm'. 非 denies a whole proposition — 'it is not the case that ——'. So this line does not say the ghosts are powerless; it takes back the suggestion the last line seemed to make and puts something narrower in its place.

神 and 人 rhyme, shén and rén — they stood in one Old Chinese rhyme group and Mandarin has kept them together, so this is one of the few places in the book where you can simply hear the verse.

sentences.t:
非其神不傷人，
聖人亦不傷人。

morph.gloss: it is not the case that
the sage — in this book the ruler who holds the Way, not a holy man
also, likewise — standing before the verb

sentences.l:
Not that their spirit-power does not harm men —
the sage too does not harm men.
sentences.i: And it is not only that their spirit-power does men no harm — the sage too does men no harm.
sentences.n:
The argument climbs by retraction: its ghosts do not work as spirits — no, rather their spirit-power does no harm — no, and not only that: the sage does no harm either. Nothing is taken from the spirits at any step; what changes each time is what is being denied.

Wang Bi draws it out symmetrically, in his note on the unit that follows: 神不傷人，聖人亦不傷人；聖人不傷人，神亦不傷人 — the spirits do not harm men, so neither does the sage; the sage does not harm men, so neither do the spirits. Which of them is the reason for which is exactly what he declines to settle.

sentences.t:
夫兩不相傷，
故德交歸焉。

morph.gloss: now, as for — the opening particle (fú)
the two of them — here the spirits and the sage
one another, mutually — set before a verb: 'harm each other'
potency — the power a thing has by being what it is
from each side, both ways — 交 is to cross, and here it is adverbial: each to the other
to go back where one belongs, to come home
in it, to it, there — the fused 於之, a real pronoun with its preposition swallowed

sentences.l:
Now the two do not harm each other,
and so potency, from each side, comes home there.
sentences.i: Neither harms the other, and so potency comes home from them both.
sentences.n:
焉 has two jobs and only position tells them apart. Here it is the fused 於之, 'to it, there' — a pronoun with its preposition swallowed, exactly as in chapter 34's 萬物歸焉, 'the ten thousand things come home to it'. Chapter 15's 豫焉 is the other job, where 焉 stands inside the line and carries nothing but its fall.

Where the potency comes home to, the text leaves open. Wang Bi supplies it: 神聖合道，交歸之也 — spirits and sage both fall in with the Way, and both alike revert to it. Read it the other way and the potency converges on the people, from the unseen powers and the ruler at once. The English above keeps both standing; 交 is the pivot, 'from each side'.
